jokes.text: I only kissed Jeff because I wanted to see if I could do it because I wanna be cool and sexy like you. / I can't believe how gross I am. / I only slept with Jeff because I hate myself, and that's why I got after you for raising money. I'm twice as gross.
jokes.setup: Annie and Britta are making up after their oil-wrestling fight with sincere self-examinations
jokes.punchline: Their competitive self-loathing escalates — first Annie's 'I can't believe how gross I am,' then Britta raises to 'I'm twice as gross' — continuing their earlier competitive dynamic but now applied to self-deprecation
jokes.explanation: Smart character comedy — the competitive dynamic between Annie and Britta is so ingrained that even their reconciliation becomes a competition (at self-criticism). 'I'm twice as gross' landing on Britta who actually slept with Jeff vs. Annie who only kissed him is both accurate and funny.

jokes.text: Because... men are even grosser? / And when we forget that, they win.
jokes.setup: They're trying to understand why oil wrestling raised more money than their earnest fundraising
jokes.punchline: Britta reduces all of gender politics to 'men are even grosser / when we forget that, they win' — an oversimplified feminist slogan delivered with total conviction
jokes.explanation: Good Britta line — it's simultaneously her genuine worldview and a parody of reductive feminist sloganeering. 'They win' as the ultimate consequence of forgetting men's grossness is both sincerely meant and funny in its simplicity. Character-specific.

jokes.text: Oh, so you got actual ice cream. / Yeah. With peanut butter and hot fudge. / What the hell, right? Nobody lives forever. / No offense. / Nah, think what you want. It's a free country.
jokes.setup: Jeff has bought actual ice cream after the failed morgue expedition
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'What the hell, right? Nobody lives forever' applied to eating peanut butter and hot fudge ice cream is funny because it's his entire existential crisis reduced to caloric indulgence — then 'No offense' to Pierce (whose mom just died/didn't die), and Pierce's breezy response
jokes.explanation: Good thematic resolution joke. Jeff's existential crisis ends in ice cream, which is both defeating and life-affirming. 'No offense' to the man whose mother just died (or didn't, per Pierce) is a nice beat, and Pierce's 'It's a free country' shows his complete disconnect from his own situation. Satisfying emotional landing.

jokes.text: Oh, so you got actual ice cream. / Yeah. With peanut butter and hot fudge. / What the hell, right? Nobody lives forever. / No offense. / Nah, think what you want. It's a free country.
jokes.setup: Jeff has bought actual ice cream, indulging his cholesterol concerns for the first time.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Nobody lives forever' and Pierce's 'No offense' / Jeff's 'Nah, think what you want. It's a free country' — the whole exchange playing against the episode's mortality theme with a weirdly warm Pierce response.
jokes.explanation: Good thematic callback. Jeff eating ice cream as his acceptance of mortality is literalized as a dessert choice. Pierce's 'No offense' (re: nobody lives forever — a potential reference to his dead mother) and Jeff's 'think what you want, it's a free country' — his version of respecting Pierce's beliefs — is a quietly well-constructed emotional beat with a comedic exterior.

jokes.text: I barely saw you this week, Abed. What have you been up to? / Not much. / Hmm. / What? / Whoa! Busted! 25 feet! Which puts you in violation of this restraining order I filed against you for abusing me with your restraining order!
jokes.setup: An apparently innocuous conversation between Shirley and Abed reveals that Abed has been secretly tracking Duncan, leading to Duncan bursting in with a counter-restraining order.
jokes.punchline: 'I filed against you for abusing me with your restraining order!' — the meta-legal absurdity of a restraining order against the enforcement of a restraining order.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a masterclass in running-gag payoff. The restraining order thread was seeded at 05:22, deployed as a force field at 14:07, and now pays off with a counter-restraining order filed for 'abusing me with your restraining order.' The meta-legal logic — that a restraining order can be weaponized, and that the response is an identical weapon — is absurd but internally consistent. 'Mutually assured destruction' as the conclusion elevates it further. This is the best payoff to a running joke in the episode. High impact in a room.

jokes.text: I barely saw you this week, Abed. What have you been up to? / Not much. / Hmm. / What? / Whoa! Busted! 25 feet!
jokes.setup: Jeff makes small talk with Abed at the end of the episode; Duncan appears and suddenly measures distance
jokes.punchline: Duncan has filed a counter-restraining order against Jeff — the '25 feet' (the same distance from Abed's earlier fill-in) is now being used against Jeff by Duncan
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. The setup was planted early (Abed knowing the '25 feet' distance), and the payoff is Duncan turning the weapon against Jeff. '25 feet!' as a triumphant exclamation lands because we know the number and understand its significance. The escalation to 'mutually assured destruction' is both funny and apt. Well-constructed, well-paced callback comedy.

jokes.text: Which puts you in violation of this restraining order I filed against you for abusing me with your restraining order!
jokes.setup: Jeff has a restraining order against Duncan; Duncan has now filed one against Jeff for using the restraining order against him
jokes.punchline: The meta-absurdity of a restraining order filed for the abuse of a restraining order — legal machinery turned on itself
jokes.explanation: Absurdist legal escalation that lands well. The specific logic of 'abusing me with your restraining order' is funny because it's both legally coherent (you can weaponize legal tools) and completely self-referential. Good structure for a callback payoff.

jokes.text: Mutually assured destruction.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Duncan have both filed restraining orders against each other, arriving at a stalemate
jokes.punchline: Abed summarizes the entire Cold War arms race analogy in two words — delivered with his signature clinical detachment as if narrating a documentary
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy. 'Mutually assured destruction' applied to a petty restraining order dispute is funny because it's both wildly disproportionate and exactly accurate as a Cold War analogy for the standoff. Only Abed would frame it this way, and only Abed would deliver it with this precise neutrality. Two words that do the work of a full comedic monologue. Near-perfect character integration and economy. This is what Abed is FOR in this show.

jokes.text: Well played, Chang. / Thank you. / Uh... That means a lot.
jokes.setup: Duncan has successfully countered Jeff's restraining order; Chang was apparently involved or observing
jokes.punchline: 'That means a lot' — Chang receives a minor compliment from a person who barely knows him with disproportionate emotional sincerity
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny Chang moment. The 'That means a lot' beat suggests Chang's emotional hunger for validation, which is characterful. Not a highlight but a good button for the scene.

jokes.text: Do you mind getting a quick photo of me with the oily coeds? / Center button. / You're the man. / Yeah, no problem. / Wha... whaaaat?
jokes.setup: Duncan has just 'won' the restraining order standoff
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks Jeff to photograph him with the oil-covered Britta and Annie — using his victory to request a service from the person he just defeated
jokes.explanation: Good Duncan character moment — his victory lap is immediately asking for a creepy photo. 'You're the man' while asking his enemy for a favor is a nice detail. 'Wha... whaaaat?' from Jeff is a good reaction to the absurdity. Solid close for the Duncan subplot.

jokes.text: He's not a projection. He's the British guy pretending to be Tom Berenger. / It was a mislead. That's the whole point of inception. Subversion of reality. / He hasn't seen it yet!
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are apparently discussing Inception and whether something is a projection or a character
jokes.punchline: Their debate about Inception spoilers lands when a student hasn't seen the film yet, and their casual deep-dive has apparently spoiled it — 'He hasn't seen it yet!' as the horrified revelation
jokes.explanation: Good Troy and Abed ending beat. Their casual deep-analysis of a film in a public space while spoiling it for a bystander is a perfect character note. 'He hasn't seen it yet!' as the punchline works because it's the absolute last concern in a conversation that never registered the other person. Good character integration — only Troy and Abed have this relationship to movies.

tmdb_overview: A death provokes a fierce debate about Pierce's religious beliefs. Britta and Annie are at odds over tactics in the Gulf oil spill fund-raising drive.
insight: Absurdist comedy carries 81-point episode on 2.7 jokes-per-minute foundation.
